key_terms.meaning: A human-readable string, such as /data/marks.csv, that a system resolves into something it can act on
The step-by-step process of turning a name into the address of the object it refers to
A name written from the global root, so it means the same thing at every site
The local directory where a remote file system is attached so its files appear under it
The set of nodes visited while a name is resolved, from the starting directory to the object
A second name stored in a directory that points to the same file identifier, so the file survives until the last link is removed
A file that holds another file's name as text; resolution restarts at that name, and the link breaks if the target goes
The file stays on the server and every read or write is sent over the network; no client copy is kept
Splitting a relation into pieces (horizontal by rows, vertical by columns) that are stored at different sites
Send only the join column of R to S, let S return matching rows, then join locally — cheaper when few rows match
Atomic commit protocol: coordinator asks all sites to prepare, then tells them all to commit or all to abort
The site that drives a distributed transaction and records the decision in its log before broadcasting it
Infrastructure as a Service: the provider rents virtual machines, storage and network; the customer runs the OS upward
Software as a Service: the provider runs the whole application and the customer only uses it through a browser or API
Software that runs several virtual machines on one physical machine by trapping privileged instructions and emulating them
The CPU switch from guest code back into the hypervisor when the guest executes a trapped or privileged instruction
Hardware that translates guest virtual to guest physical to host physical addresses in one walk, avoiding shadow tables
Copying a running VM's memory to another host while it keeps serving, then switching over in a short pause
The headroom a design allows: how far load can grow before adding resources stops helping linearly
Automatic, short-term acquisition and release of resources to match demand, billed for the time used

takeaways: A distributed file system hides the network by resolving names to locations and by choosing, per file, whether to cache and how to keep cached copies fresh.
Hard links point to a file identifier and survive renaming; soft links point to a name and break when the target moves.
The remote access model is always fresh but slow; the caching model is fast but needs a consistency rule for stale copies.
A distributed query is fragmented and pushed to the sites holding the data, and the winning plan is the one that ships the fewest bytes.
Semijoins beat full shipping when the join column is small and few rows match.
Two-phase commit gives all-or-nothing across sites at the cost of blocking while the coordinator's decision is unknown.
The cloud service model fixes the split of responsibility: IaaS leaves you the OS, PaaS leaves you the code, SaaS leaves you only the data.
A hypervisor turns a server into a file, which is what makes snapshots, cloning, consolidation and live migration possible.
Scalability is a property of the design; elasticity is an operating policy that buys capacity for minutes and returns it.
A grid federates machines owned by different organisations under shared protocols while each site keeps its own policy.
Web systems trade freshness for latency: caches, replicas and indexes are why stale reads are a design decision, not a bug.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually built around one diagram plus a comparison table, so practise drawing the layered picture (name to address, coordinator to participants, guest to hypervisor to host) and then arguing a trade-off in words.

bank.q: Explain how a name is resolved to an address in a distributed file system, using a path such as /home/me/notes.txt as the running example. Distinguish absolute from relative names and name from address.
outline: Start at the root or at the client's working directory for a relative name
Each component is looked up in a directory table; the directory holds name, identifier or address
Iterative resolution: the client asks each server in turn
Recursive resolution: the first server does the chasing and returns the address
Caching of the last resolution shortens later paths; state the freshness problem of cached entries
Closure: the same name resolves identically at every site in the closure of the name

bank.q: Compare the remote access model with the caching model of a distributed file system. How does each model decide where a client's data lives? Discuss the cache consistency problem and one protocol to solve it.
outline: Remote access model: file stays on server, every operation is an RPC, always fresh, high latency
Caching model: copy brought to client, reads local, faster, needs invalidation or write-through
Client-initiated versus server-initiated consistency
Lease or callback invalidation, or time-based staleness bound
Open-file sharing semantics: UNIX versus session semantics
Choose a model for a read-heavy intranet file share and justify

bank.q: Describe the two-phase commit protocol. Give the messages, the states each participant passes through, and what happens when a participant or the coordinator fails.
outline: Phase 1: coordinator sends prepare; participant votes yes (and writes to log) or no
Phase 2: coordinator logs the decision and sends commit or abort to all
Participant states: initial, ready, committed, aborted
Failure of a participant before voting: coordinator aborts
Failure after voting yes: participant blocks until the decision is known
Coordinator failure: participants may block; presumed abort versus presumed commit
Termination and recovery protocol with the coordinator's log

bank.q: Define cloud computing and list its essential characteristics, the three service models and the four deployment models.
outline: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service
IaaS, PaaS, SaaS with one example each
Public, private, hybrid, community
Pay-per-use metering as the economic definition of utility computing
One line on the trade-off that comes with each deployment model

bank.q: Explain how a hypervisor virtualises a CPU. Cover privileged instructions, traps, VM exit, binary translation or paravirtualisation, and hardware-assisted virtualisation.
outline: Guest runs in a less privileged ring; privileged instructions must not act on real hardware
Trap-and-emulate: instruction traps, hypervisor emulates it, returns to guest
VM exit and VM entry overhead
Binary translation: rewrite guest code blocks ahead of time to avoid traps
Paravirtualisation: guest is modified to make hypercalls instead of privileged instructions
Hardware extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) add a guest mode and a virtual machine control structure
Cost of exits is why I/O-heavy guests need help such as paravirtual drivers

bank.q: Relation R has 1,000,000 rows and S has 10,000 rows, stored at different sites. R.a = S.a, and the join column is 8 bytes while a full row is 200 bytes. Compute the data shipped for a full transfer plan, for a semijoin R ⋉ S, and for a semijoin with a Bloom filter, and state which plan wins.
outline: Ship S to R: 10,000 × 200 = 2 MB
Semijoin: send R's join column, 1,000,000 × 8 = 8 MB; S returns matching rows
Compare against shipping S whole, and note the break-even point
Bloom filter shrinks the join column to a few bits per row at the cost of false positives
State the assumption about how many rows actually match

bank.q: A query joins a 1 GB table at site A with a 50 MB table at site B, and the network between them moves 100 Mbps. Estimate the transfer time for each plan, then explain how a cost-based optimiser would pick one, and where this runs in a cloud deployment where the two tables sit in different regions.
outline: Convert sizes to bits; time = size ÷ bandwidth
1 GB at 100 Mbps ≈ 80 s; 50 MB ≈ 4 s
Add per-row CPU cost and any disk cost at the site
Selectivity estimate changes the decision; histogram or sampling
Region-to-region egress is metered, so bandwidth cost is part of the plan cost
Co-locating the fragments removes the transfer but adds a one-off copy cost

bank.q: Design an auto-scaling policy for a ticketing site that sells cricket match tickets. Specify the metric, the thresholds, the cool-down periods and the instance mix, and explain why buying capacity by the minute matters here.
outline: Metric: CPU utilisation, request rate or queue length; pick one and justify
Scale out when the metric exceeds the high threshold for N consecutive periods
Scale in slowly with a longer cool-down to avoid thrashing
Min and max bounds so cost stays predictable
Warm-up time of an instance means you must scale before the load, not after
Metered billing means the idle overnight hours cost nothing
Add a load balancer and health checks so new instances actually receive traffic

bank.q: A web application serves a product catalogue. Explain how you would combine caching, replication and indexing to serve pages in a few tens of milliseconds, and how you would bound the staleness a shopper can see.
outline: Read-through cache in front of the database, with a time-to-live per item
Replicate the catalogue to several read replicas in different regions
Index the searchable columns; keep the index on the same node as the data
Invalidate on write, or publish a new version and let old versions expire
Explicit staleness bound, for example a price is at most 60 s old
Read-your-own-writes for a customer who just edited the cart
Push static assets to a content delivery network

bank.q: Explain, with a small directory example, how hard links and soft links behave when the target file is renamed, deleted, and restored. Then explain what a mount point does when a remote file system is attached to a client.
outline: Directory entry maps name to a file identifier (inode number in UNIX terms)
Hard link: new directory entry, same identifier, link count grows; delete decrements the count
Hard link survives a rename because it names the identifier, not the path
Hard links cannot cross file systems
Soft link stores a text path; resolution restarts at the target's path, so it breaks on rename or delete
Mount point: remote file system's root is attached to a local directory; lookup below it forwards to the server
Absolute versus relative names interacting with mount points

bank.q: A distributed transactions workload runs across four sites on a cloud with occasional virtual machine restarts. Analyse how two-phase commit, replication and live migration interact when the coordinator's host is migrated during phase 2, and state what guarantee survives.
outline: Coordinator's log must be durable on shared storage before it broadcasts a decision
Live migration preserves the VM's state, so the broadcast continues after the switch
If the coordinator genuinely crashes, participants block after a yes vote
Three-phase commit or a replicated coordinator removes the single point of blocking
Replication of the log converts one coordinator into a quorum
Atomicity survives; liveness may not, and the answer must say which is which

bank.q: A start-up with three developers must deploy a new application with unpredictable load. Evaluate the choice between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS for their situation, and state how virtualisation underneath supports your choice.
outline: Define the responsibility boundary of each model
IaaS: full control, most operational work, needs an administrator
PaaS: the provider patches the runtime and the OS, the team ships code
SaaS: least work, least control, fits only if the application is standard
Small team and unpredictable load favour PaaS plus managed database
Virtualisation gives the provider cheap isolation, snapshots and migration, which is why small units of compute can be rented
Cost model: pay for usage, but beware network egress and idle managed services
State the exit path so the team is not locked in

bank.q: Compare a grid and a cloud for a research group that must run a week-long simulation over data held by five partner institutes. Cover ownership, trust, scheduling, fault tolerance and elasticity.
outline: Grid: machines owned by each institute, shared protocols, each site keeps its own policy and identity
Cloud: provider owns the hardware, the customer rents and trusts the provider
Scheduling: grid brokers across administrative domains, with local queues; a cloud allocates instances directly
Fault tolerance: grid jobs checkpoint and restart, since nodes are donated and may vanish; the cloud offers the same via migration and restart
Elasticity: cloud can add a thousand cores for an hour, the grid cannot
Data: in a grid, data usually stays where its owner put it, so move the job to the data
Choose the grid where governance requires the data and machines to stay with the institutes

bank.q: Cloud monitoring shows a service that scales out correctly but leaks a stale cache entry for exactly the value that drives autoscaling. Evaluate the risk to availability and propose safeguards.
outline: Describe the feedback loop: metric, scaling decision, action, re-measure
A stale metric can trigger scale-in while load is high, causing overload
Use a windowed aggregate, not the latest sample; require consecutive breaches
Keep a hard minimum instance count as a floor
Health checks and load balancer removal before termination
Cross-check with an independent signal such as request rate
Alert on the feedback loop itself, not only on the metric

bank.q: You must choose between replication of data and live migration of virtual machines to survive a host failure. Evaluate both for a 100 GB database that must stay available, and say where each is the better tool.
outline: Replication: keep a second up-to-date copy at another host, failover in seconds, application-level consistency rules needed
Migration: moves a running VM, does not protect against host failure by itself
Migration is for maintenance and packing, replication is for fault tolerance
Cost of 100 GB: full copy over the network versus continuous log shipping
Synchronous versus asynchronous replication and the latency it adds
Recovery objectives: recovery time and recovery point
Combine: replicate for availability, migrate for planned maintenance

glossary.def: The location information a system really uses to reach an object, such as a server plus a local file identifier.
An internal, location-independent handle for a file or object; a name is resolved to it, and the identifier never needs to change.
A name interpreted from the client's current directory rather than from the global root.
The fixed-size units a file server transfers; a file's size and access pattern decide how many block transfers a read costs.
A directory entry holding a text path to another file; resolution restarts at that path, so the link breaks if the target moves.
An atomic commit protocol that adds a pre-commit phase so participants are not blocked by a single coordinator failure, at more message rounds.
The correctness rule that the outcome of interleaved transactions equals some serial order of them.
Platform as a Service: the provider runs the OS and runtime; the customer supplies code and data.
Cloud technology operated for one organisation, on its own or rented hardware, with self-service and metering inside it.
Two clouds of different kinds joined by enough portability that workloads and data can move between them.
One running instance serves many customers whose data is kept apart by software, sharing the cost of the hardware.
A hypervisor running directly on the hardware, with guest operating systems above it.
Virtualisation where the guest is modified to make hypercalls instead of executing trapped privileged instructions.
A deliberate call from a paravirtualised guest into the hypervisor, cheaper than a trap and emulate round.
Software-maintained tables that map guest virtual addresses straight to host physical addresses, kept in step with the guest's own tables.
A point-in-time copy of a virtual machine's disk and memory state, used as a restore point or as a base for clones.
A Linux kernel feature that limits and accounts the CPU, memory and I/O a group of processes may use, forming the basis of containers.
A Linux kernel feature that gives a process its own view of process IDs, network, mounts and hostname, so it cannot see other tenants.
A control loop that adds or removes instances to keep a chosen metric inside its thresholds.
A component that spreads incoming requests over a set of instances and stops sending to unhealthy ones.
A set of people and sites from different organisations who share resources under agreed rules for the life of a project.
The software layer that handles authentication across sites, job submission, data movement and resource discovery in a grid.
A read that returns an older value than the latest committed write, because it was served from a cache or a replica.
A set of caches placed close to users that serve copies of static content and shorten the network path.
